The example of a body becoming white assumes that whiteness comes from outside. It does not show that a necessary consequence can be separate from the essence it follows.
The author means that a simple source may be both the source and the basis of what follows from it, without being divided into a giver and a receiver.

A human soul begins as an intellect in potential and receives forms over time. A being that is always fully actual has no such receptive stage; the very forms that follow from it may be both caused and present in it.

If this statement comes from someone who holds, like the author, that God's utterly simple reality contains all existence in a higher way, its meaning is this: God's greatness lies in knowing Himself, and in that same knowledge knowing everything else. His knowledge gathers all things into one without losing their distinct details.

Those who explain divine knowledge through separate forms usually accept a simpler and more general knowledge in God's essence. The forms do not add perfection to Him. Rather, they proceed from His essence, which already possesses perfection at a higher level.

If the statement comes from someone who does not accept the author's full view, it has another sense. God's greatness does not depend on knowing forms or external things merely as objects outside Him. It lies in His bringing things forth as intelligible realities, considered in their relation to Him as lights and knowledge. In that respect they depend entirely on Him; His perfection does not come from something other than Himself.

An objection may be raised: do not all these thinkers already agree that God's simple essence contains knowledge of everything? Why present this view as the special insight of only a few? The reply is that a conclusion may follow from someone's teaching without that thinker ever noticing it—or even being willing to accept it if it were pointed out. The same implication might be drawn from ordinary statements that God is self-sufficient and knows Himself and others. But explicitly recognising and proving that His single knowledge is detailed, not merely general, is a further claim. The author therefore treats it as a discovery shared with a few earlier masters of philosophy.

“Receive,” “be completed by,” and “be described by” can each suggest a different problem: change over time, dependence on another, or added qualities. None applies to forms that arise from God's essence without making Him more complete. — س قده

Avicenna's followers do not all explain the point in the same way as the author. The forms are not divine perfections because of their meanings as concepts; they are God's detailed knowledge insofar as they arise from His own essence, without an outside cause or receiver.
The author reads Avicenna to mean that God's knowledge of Himself entails the existence of these forms. Since His self-knowledge is direct, it is also the source of their existence. — س قده
“An existence that can be understood” means an existence that has the capacity to be known. A separate intellect, by contrast, exists in a way that is already intelligible. — س قده
The relation is purely intellectual and dependent, not a physical relation between a form and matter or an accident and its subject. — س قده

If the forms exist from God through the same simple act by which He knows them, then they are not separate from Him in existence. This suggests a kind of union between knower and known, though the author says its exact nature is hard to grasp.
The sentence means that God is both knower and known because He knows Himself as the source of all things.

The fact that many forms come after God's essence and stand in an order of cause and effect does not remove the difficulty. The objection made by Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Ṭūsī concerns the claim that forms are qualities present in God's being, as some philosophers say when they describe them as imprinted in Him or as inseparable features joined to Him. Even if those forms make up an ordered series, if they dwell in God's being, then His being is the place in which many distinct things exist. If they do not dwell in Him but stand apart and come from Him, the account begins to resemble the separate Forms that these philosophers reject.

Those Forms, moreover, do not stand in a causal chain; thinkers of the Illuminationist school place them side by side. An ordered series of forms would not, by itself, require two separate principles in God, one to bring them forth and another to receive them, provided the necessity of the forms came from His very being and not from an outside source. But that does not resolve the main objection. The created intellects and lower things do not divide God's reality precisely because they exist in themselves, not in Him. If they were placed in Him, He would become the bearer of many things. Nor can we say that an ordered series is not really many.
Differences between higher and lower causes remain differences; the cause and what it causes cannot be simply the same thing.

God knows Himself, and knowing a cause includes knowing what follows from it. So He knows the whole. As the Qur'an asks, “Does He who created not know?” That is: does the Creator and cause of all else not know what He created? He is subtle and fully aware. He is free from matter; and, in the argument used here, every being free from matter knows itself. Knowledge of the cause therefore brings knowledge of the effect.

When al-Fārābī says that there is no multiplicity in God, he may mean His knowledge of all things in one complete act. That follows because a reality wholly without parts contains everything in a simple way, without separate pieces. Differences remain only between the meanings of the divine names and what follows from them, which are the natures of things. If instead he means God's detailed knowledge that follows this complete knowledge, as in al-Fārābī's own account, the many objects of that knowledge are understood in their proper order, as the author explains.
God's knowledge of all things is implicit in His self-knowledge; His detailed knowledge of them follows from knowing Himself as their cause. — س قده

If divine knowledge is described as detailed, saying that knowledge of all things comes 'after' knowledge of God's essence is easy enough to understand as an order of explanation. If divine knowledge is one and undivided, 'after' must mean something else. We first establish God's essence and His knowledge of Himself, then use these to establish His knowledge of all things. Or, in thought, we first consider His essence, then His being knowing, then His knowing other things. None of these stages is a change in God.

We find a similar order when reports speak of God knowing, willing, intending, measuring, decreeing, and bringing about. Mystical writers likewise speak first of the divine essence without distinction, and then of names and attributes. The order belongs to explanation, not to God's life in time.

In the sentence under discussion, 'after His essence' describes all the things whose existence is subsequent to His, rather than serving as a claim about when His knowledge occurs. The statement says that His knowledge of those things, like His knowledge of Himself, is His very essence. Some copies of the Fusus omit the words 'His very essence.'

The statement that 'all things are united in relation to His essence' can be read through either simple or detailed divine knowledge. It is especially plain on the first reading. On the second, the author's account of the order of causes shows how many things are related through one source.

The better reading is that the Teacher is explaining why an infinite range of different things does not introduce multiplicity into God's essence or His knowledge. God's one, simple existence discloses things that are many and unlike one another, because they all depend on that one stable source. Their shared dependence joins what is otherwise scattered and brings what differs into relation.

The expression 'He is all things in unity' seems to point to the principle that simple reality contains everything in a higher way. Someone might instead say that 'all things' here means the created world as one whole, since God's essence simply knows that whole. But this reading is strained, and it gives the pronouns in the passage different references. — س قده
The critic's claim that the First Effect is “in” God would prove something only if “in” meant that it inheres in Him as an accident. That is precisely what the author denies.

Avicenna argues that the forms exist through God's knowing them, and God's knowing them is not a second act added to that existence. If one were distinct from the other, the same circular dependence or endless chain would return.

This is not like the relation of physical things to God. Bodies remain because He preserves them and exist because He creates them. Their dependence is plain: matter and its features, including change, time, and place, reveal how limited and distinct they are. In the separate intellects, even these signs of limitation are almost lost. Their relation to God is closer still, although they are among His acts, not His attributes.

The author has been challenged for speaking this way about the intellects. If their everlasting existence belongs to God's own everlasting existence, the critic argues, then their being would be His being, and His being theirs. One of the author's contemporaries, Shams al-Gīlānī, quotes his discussion in The Treatise on Coming into Being and objects that a being possible in itself would then become necessary in itself.

This objection looks more like a discussion of ordinary words than a careful philosophical distinction. Those who follow the approach sometimes called the taste of divine unity hold that possible essences exist through their relation to the self-subsisting Reality. Since the relation does not exist independently, in reality everything that exists does so through God's existence. Their teachers explain this in works such as Al-Taqdīsāt. Some even say that Zayd's existence is Zayd's God. Yet they do not conclude that a possible essence has become a necessary essence. On their view, the essence remains possible, while the existence through which it is present is another matter. That is why they speak of multiplicity among existing things and unity in existence itself.

Perhaps the critic also objects to the spiritual teachers' claim that the meanings of the divine names and attributes exist through the One they name, so that a name is the same as the named Reality in one respect and different in another.
Here, likewise, the intellects have essences to which possibility belongs, while their existence comes from God. Essence and existence must not be confused. Each has its own proper account.

Even if we adopt the author's own position, according to which existence is fundamental and has levels differing in strength, the separate intellects still have no independent existence beside His. Their existence is dependent, like the meaning of a word that cannot stand alone but needs another word to complete it. One line of poetry says of such realities, “We were exalted letters that had not yet been spoken.” They show or point toward the divine essence. When something is considered only as a way of pointing to another, it has no independent standing. That is the meaning of saying the intellects belong to the divine domain and exist through God. In one respect they are not God; in another they are not entirely other than Him. The same applies to one who loses separate self-awareness in the reality contemplated.

How, I wonder, can critics accept the saying attributed to ʿAlī, the foremost of those who ascend through knowledge, “I tore off the gate of Khaybar through divine strength,” while denying this relation? And how can they accept the Qur'anic words, “You did not throw when you threw, but God threw”? — S. R.

Why does the argument speak specifically of what is first brought into being, when the same account also applies to things that are formed within the world? One answer is that the universal kinds found here are preserved as one individual succeeds another. Knowledge of particular things is then contained within knowledge of their universal kinds, as the philosophers in Aristotle’s school maintain. Another answer is that the whole of the world, considered without dividing it into separate things and in relation to the one God, is one thing issuing from the One. Scripture says, ‘Our command is but one.’ From this point of view, the whole is brought into being at once, without any prior matter or stretch of time.

Matter, time, and place already belong to the whole we are considering; they cannot stand outside it as conditions for its creation. The argument is stated in universal terms because science deals with general statements. Compare ‘Every Necessary Being is simple’ or ‘For every Necessary Being, what it is and that it is are one.’ ‘Form’ can mean either what makes something actually exist or the form grasped by the intellect. — س قده

One may object: how can the forms be without limit? The kinds of immaterial and material beings, whether heavenly or earthly, seem finite. Nor does this account assign a separate form in God to every one of infinitely many individuals. Further, if infinitely many forms are ordered as causes and effects, there seems to be an endless chain of causes bounded at either end.

There are several replies to the first objection. “Without limit” may describe their range or intensity by reference to God's unlimited light, rather than an independent infinity of forms. That is why the author says that they are eternal through His eternity. Or the basic kinds of substances and qualities may be finite while their combinations are beyond counting. There are only a few basic tastes, for example, yet their mixtures have innumerable varieties. A further possibility is that the forms of particular things exist in God, each with the features that make it a kind represented by only one individual.

The second objection assumes that the entire limitless collection forms one chain of causes. It need not. On the view that forms exist independently as dominating lights, the causal order belongs to the higher lights, not to the equal-ranking forms called exemplars. Moreover, the order extends towards the effects; it does not require an endless series leading upwards towards the first cause. — س قده
The argument denies that God's essence is multiplied when He knows many things. The many things are known through one eternal source.
“The known things” here means things as they exist outside knowledge, not the forms by which they are known. — س قده

These philosophers accept that God's perfect, all-embracing knowledge is identical with His essence and comes before particular things. That knowledge is enough when the things known are themselves forms whose very existence is detailed knowledge of them. God's giving them existence is then the same relation as His knowing them.

But they say that external material things are different. For them, the simple knowledge in God's essence is not enough to explain His detailed knowledge of things outside Him. The forms must therefore proceed from Him before those external things come to exist. The objection cannot be forced on the philosophers of illumination, since they hold that God's producing external things and His knowing them are one relation. The Aristotle’s followers disagree, relying on their rule that what is directly known must exist for the knower, not merely in matter.

A clearer way to put their argument may be this: God's existence is pure oneness and simplicity, while the many things outside Him are, by comparison, pure multiplicity. To connect the two, they posit an intermediate level that joins unity and multiplicity. This is the level of forms impressed in knowledge. The author's words can be understood in that sense. — س قده
These forms are necessary consequences of God's essence; the essence does not cause them as a separate agent causes a separate effect. — س قده

The critic's either-or argument works only if “substance” and “accident” are both taken in the same sense. A mental substance can be a real accident in the external order, so the two descriptions do not exclude each other. — س قده
The forms are substantial in meaning but exist in God as dependent qualities of knowledge. Since they are causes of external things, their effects make them more, not less, suited to be real. — س قده
The author accepts that these forms are not perfections added to God. God's perfection is His own essence, which contains all that proceeds from Him in a higher way. — س قده

This passage has two purposes. First, someone might say that al-Khafrī only meant that God's knowledge of external things through forms is not perfect knowledge belonging to His essence. If that is so, why does the author twice speak of God's knowledge of the forms in a way that seems to contradict him?

Second, one might grant that reading of al-Khafrī but still argue that God's knowledge of external things follows from the production of the forms. The reply is that God's knowledge of the forms is the very knowledge through which He knows the external things. In much the same way, knowing an image of the sun is a way of knowing the sun itself: the image is how we direct our attention to what it represents. We can distinguish what is known directly from what is known through it, but that does not give us two separate acts of knowledge or prove that one act comes after the other.

Likewise, there is no difference here between knowing by means of the forms and knowing the forms themselves. We therefore need not force the word “by” in the passage to mean “because of”; it can simply connect “knowledge” with its object. — س قده

The comparison with Suhrawardī is only partial. Suhrawardī says the presence of things themselves is God's direct knowledge; al-Tusi instead makes forms in higher intellects or souls the basis of that knowledge.
The objection to this account has already been explained: material things do not become intellectual forms in themselves before they are abstracted from matter.
A consequence that follows from an essence follows it in both ways of existing. It cannot exist in the world while its essence exists only in the mind, or vice versa. — س قده

It would be better to direct the objection at two claims: that the forms impressed upon the intellect are effects of the Necessary Being, and that knowledge acquired through representations belongs to the qualities of the soul.

If we grant both claims, those impressed forms have a kind of existence outside the mere act of thinking. In that respect they are real features, as other qualities of the soul are. Their necessary connection with God concerns what they are, as existing qualities whose existence depends on the Necessary Being. It does not arise simply because they are ideas in a mind, or because they have such-and-such a mental content.

The First Being cannot be present in a mind as a mental image. He is pure reality, not something that can enter any mind and become an idea. Nor do the consequences that necessarily follow from Him need Him to be an object inside our thought. On the argument being discussed, they must therefore be real things rather than merely mental things.

But this reasoning can be challenged by our own mental forms. Suppose the forms in our minds were properties of essences simply as essences. They would have to belong to those essences whether or not anything existed—an obviously false result. Suppose instead that they were “mental properties.” Would our souls then have to exist inside another mind before those properties could belong to them? That is also absurd. The argument would leave only the claim that our mental images are external properties, which contradicts what it set out to prove.

The answer is that all these forms are real in themselves, because they belong to a soul that exists in reality. A feature of a real being is itself real. We call them “mental” only in comparison with the other real beings they represent. In the case of God, philosophers use “mental” for forms said to be present in divine knowledge, and “external” for beings that have their own standing or are present in matter, where one thing is absent from another. Indeed, by the usual test of whether something produces effects, the forms in divine knowledge would have a stronger claim to be called real: they are understood as sources of the things that appear in the world. — س قده

One defence of the rule says that knowing a cause directly must bring with it direct knowledge of the effect. On that reading, the rule supports the view that God's knowledge is detailed and immediately present even while it is one complete act. It would not support the view held by Aristotle’s followers that He knows things through separate representations.

But there is a difficulty with that reading. The rule was discussed by the philosophers in Aristotle’s school in the part of logic concerned with demonstration. They did not generally accept direct knowledge except in the case of a thing knowing itself. Moreover, demonstration works through ideas and judgments, not through immediate presence. If the rule applied only to direct awareness, the logical distinction between proofs that move from cause to effect and proofs that move from effect to cause would lose its purpose.

Avicenna and other Aristotle’s followers therefore do not grant that a cause's knowledge of its effect, or an effect's knowledge of its cause, must be immediate awareness. Nor do they take this rule to establish that claim.

Direct knowledge of another thing can come through union with it or through being its cause and encompassing it in existence. The author's claim is that God's knowledge of created existences works in this second way. — س قده

One might object that, even if existence itself is what God brings into being, the rule that knowledge of a cause brings knowledge of its effects establishes only that He knows those effects somehow. Why must His knowledge be direct rather than through representations?

The answer is that existence has no single fixed manner of being and no essence that could be represented by a separate image. An image represents the nature of an existing thing, not existence itself. To know a particular existence as such is therefore to know it by its presence. The author's point is that the rule used by everyone to establish that God knows other things also establishes how He knows them: directly, not through forms impressed upon a knower, as some thinkers maintain.

A second objection follows. Earlier, the author seemed to criticize Suhrawardi, Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, and others who regard existing things themselves as God's knowledge. He suggested that they had overlooked a familiar principle: for something directly perceived, its existence in itself and its existence as perceived are one. Material existence, however, is normally concealed from perception, while knowledge requires presence and disclosure. Why does he now seem to endorse the view he earlier challenged?

In the earlier passage, he was explaining why the philosophers who rely on mental forms had adopted their position. Their rule made it difficult to call material things directly present to God. The thinkers who defended direct knowledge might not have accepted that rule, or they might have held that material things are not hidden from God. His knowledge embraces matter as well as everything else. Things with position and direction remain what they are, but before Him they are all equally present, as though gathered into a point.

Here the author's task is different. He uses the established rule about knowing effects through their cause to reject knowledge by impressed forms and to support knowledge through presence. The main purpose is to challenge the theory of representations, not simply to repeat an earlier proof. — س قده
These existences may be called God's knowledge because they are one with His knowledge in existence, and their being known is considered before their being made.

The author adds a fourth objection to mental forms: image-based knowledge belongs to souls that perceive through sense and intellect. Separate beings that are free of matter know through direct presence, not mental concepts. — ط مد ظله

The author has briefly used a principle of his own—that existence itself is what is brought about, and that it is known by direct presence—to criticize the approach of the philosophers of illumination. He now turns to the proof that Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Tusi gave for that approach, a proof he regards as persuasive rather than decisive.

But the heart of al-Tusi's argument is sound: if two causes are one, their immediate effects must also be one. Otherwise, many things would come directly from one source. In this case, there would be the forms arising from God's knowledge of Himself, which is identical with His being, and then the things corresponding to those forms, arising from His being again.

Perhaps the author took al-Tusi to be arguing merely from a likeness between cause and effect: because the causes are one, it would be fitting for the effects to be one as well. That is not the force of the argument.
The forms follow from God's essence without existing later than it. They exist and remain through His existence and permanence, rather than being separately produced.

God's knowledge must belong to His divine reality, not to a world outside it. If Plato's Forms were external beings, they too would need prior knowledge and the same question would repeat. Properly understood, the Platonic view can be brought close to the account here.

Al-Fārābī's reconciliation treats divine Forms as present in God without being spatial shapes or separate worlds. This avoids the claim that God creates blindly or at random, while also avoiding an external realm of images. — س قده

If the divine forms were not connected to God's knowledge, one might treat them as separate realities existing on their own. But that would not make them ghostly images or bodies occupying places outside our world. They could instead be the inward realities of this world, not another set of objects beside it. Nor would that alone require infinitely many worlds.

One interpretation of the Platonic Forms, discussed in the First Journey, treats them as independently existing measurable images, one for each particular member of each kind. The Teacher's point is that the divine forms should be understood as forms of knowledge, not as extended figures. If they were figures belonging to matter, they would be bodies, and bodies need places. This would put other bodily worlds alongside ours. Aristotle objected to such worlds, among other reasons because of the empty spaces they would require, as in the problem of two spheres touching at a single point.

An endless series would follow as well. Each bodily world would have to be preceded by knowledge of it. But if that knowledge were itself a collection of separate, measurable bodies, it would make another world in need of yet earlier knowledge. There would be no end.

There is another possible reading. Suppose the divine forms were not intellects and forms of knowledge belonging to the divine realm, standing inwardly and above this world. Suppose instead that they were separate intellects occupying a place outside it, alongside it, while the natural kinds here were not their shadows or effects. Such intellects would still act and produce natural forms. Just as things in this lower world reflect higher realities, these supposed intellects would produce lower worlds. Since these forms would themselves constitute a possible world, that world too would need earlier forms of knowledge, and so on without end.

The issue is not that each divine form must be a whole world and that there are infinitely many forms. Rather, each world of forms is supposed to be preceded by another such world. On this reading, calling the forms 'images' means that they disclose the things beneath them. Describing them as being in places outside the world is a way of saying that they stand alongside it rather than above it in the order of causes. The first reading, however, seems the clearer one.

Their argument says that God's essence is what distinguishes each thing, and that whatever distinguishes a thing is knowledge of it. The second claim is the converse of “knowledge is what distinguishes a thing,” so the argument needs that reversal to be valid. — س قده

The author says the argument as first reported has a different structure and does not rely on reversing the claim about knowledge and distinction. The wording may mean that the second argument is only a restatement of the first.

These thinkers focus on essences and general concepts. One concept cannot be another, so knowledge of one concept cannot be the same as knowledge of all concepts. If the focus is existence itself, however, one simple knowledge may contain detailed knowledge.

If they understood that this oneness is true unity, not the numerical unity of one thing set against another, they would see the point. Every thing has a face turned toward God and a face turned toward itself. These two faces are not combined as one independent thing is combined with another, but more as an object is related to its shadow. A Persian verse says, in effect: “You are a radiant sun, and I am the shadow it casts in the west; the shadow's coming and going depend on the sun.” When the sun of truth rises, the passing appearances fade and all faces bow before the Living, the Sustainer.

We have already established, in discussing existence and essence, that a thing's existence is simply the reality of that thing. Its essence does not become real in any other way. Consider blackness. As a meaning, it is blackness; as something real, it exists. But the actual occurrence of blackness is not a second thing added to a blackness that already existed. What was supposedly awaiting this addition would itself have no determinate reality. The actual blackness is one instance of existence. Reality deserves the name “real” more fully than anything that becomes real only through it.

The difference, then, is between qualities within one reality, not a separation between two independent things. As the Qur'an says of invented gods, “They are only names that you and your fathers have named, for which God has sent down no authority.” The objection that prompted these remarks may therefore be met by distinguishing a thing's true existence from the names and descriptions we attach to it. — س قده
The argument has addressed the problem on the side of the knower—how one simple essence can know many things. It now raises the problem on the side of the things known: they do not yet exist. — س قده
This refers to the Muʿtazilite claim that nonexistent things have a kind of reality before they exist.

The reply is that a thing can be distinguished by what makes it the thing it is, just as it can be distinguished by its mental form. The thing's relation to a receiver is possible; its relation to the source that brings it about is necessary.
The commentator objects that a cause and its effect must have some likeness or shared nature; otherwise, one cannot explain how one produces the other. — س قده

A mental form represents the thing known, either by sharing its nature or by resembling it. A cause is neither the nature nor a likeness of its effect. The relation between cause and effect is more complex when existence, rather than essence, is considered. — س قده

This seems to contradict the first reply, which said that what gives a thing its character distinguishes it. The commentator reconciles them by saying that the first reply concerns differences among the known things, while this answer concerns the absence of differences within the one act of knowledge. — س قده

If “human nature” means an essence with properties added to it, then the claimed inclusion is false. The better reading is the complete intellectual human reality, which gathers all the levels and perfections found in human beings. Its implications follow from its existence without coming later in time. — س قده

For example, one may understand divine light as present and manifest, while also imagining physical light, its spread, extension, and duration in time. The mind understands the spiritual meaning while imagination supplies a bodily picture.
